problem: Existing interactive embodied-AI simulators run at only about 10-400 steps/s. Earlier rearrangement benchmarks either used static scans, abstracted manipulation away with 'magic' pick actions, or covered single-object, container-free tasks. This made large-scale RL on long-horizon, home-scale mobile manipulation with articulated containers impractical.
motivation: Training home-assistant robots on hardware is slow, expensive and hard to reproduce, so the full stack has to exist in simulation: interactive data, fast physics plus rendering, and reproducible tasks. The authors note that general-purpose engines and Python 'homebrew' integrations waste orders of magnitude of throughput. A lazy, tightly integrated C++ simulator with about 100x speedup would turn 6-month experiments into 2-day ones and allow a systematic comparison of RL against classical sense-plan-act pipelines.
key_idea: Build a deliberately 'lazy' rigid-body simulator that trades breadth for speed. It uses localized physics, interleaved CPU physics / GPU rendering with a one-step observation delay, and asset simplification and reuse. The simulator is paired with an artist-authored interactive apartment dataset (ReplicaCAD) and a GeometricGoal rearrangement task suite (HAB), which is used to compare flat RL, hierarchical RL skills and SPA pipelines.
insight: Simulator speed comes from not simulating what is unnecessary. The ablation in Table 2 shows single-process idle SPS falling from 1191 to 242 when all optimizations are removed; physics optimizations matter most in Idle, rendering optimizations most in Interact. On the tasks, a flat end-to-end RL policy learns individual skills but cannot chain them over thousands of steps. A perfect STRIPS task planner plus RL skills works far better, yet suffers 'hand-off' failures: a skill leaves the robot badly positioned, or a drawer only partly open, for the next skill. The gap between learned and oracle navigation shows that navigating *for* manipulation, to a non-unique, suitable pose given only the object's 3D position, is a key bottleneck; learned termination alone costs about 20% nav-skill success. SPA matches or beats RL in easy, uncluttered settings but is brittle: it needs the whole workspace mapped from egocentric views, so it degrades in the cluttered fridge and after imperfect navigation. Surprisingly, blind proprioception-only pick policies reach 78% success by 'feeling their way'.
method: ReplicaCAD dataset: an artist recreation of the Replica FRL-apartment. It has 92 objects with physical parameters, collision proxies, articulation URDFs (fridge, drawers) and annotated support surfaces and containment volumes. There are 5 artist macro-variations x 20 micro-variations (111 layouts in total) plus offline-computed procedural YCB clutter.

Localized physics and rendering: only the robot applies non-gravitational forces, so distant objects are not updated. The base moves kinematically on a navmesh, sleeping objects reuse cached transforms and culling, and parts rigidly attached to a base are treated as static.

Interleaved physics/rendering: the policy acts on the previous observation, pi(a_t | o_{t-1}). This lets Bullet physics on the CPU (s_{t+1}) run in parallel with Magnum rendering on the GPU (o_t), and adds realistic sensing latency.

Simplify and reuse: Basis GPU texture compression (4-6x memory reduction), prefetching and instancing of cached assets to speed up resets, and convex-decomposition collision meshes kept separate from visual meshes. OMPL motion planning is integrated for SPA baselines.

Task setup: a Fetch robot with head and arm RGB-D cameras (128x128), proprioception and egomotion. It uses end-effector delta control at 30 Hz (max 1.5 cm/step, IK plus PD), abstracted grasp (snaps to the nearest object within 15 cm) and base velocity control. Goals follow the GeometricGoal format (start and target 3D centers of mass); success means every object is within 15 cm, and a pick fails if accumulated contact force exceeds 5k N.

Baselines: MonolithicRL is a CNN + proprioception/goal encoder + LSTM actor-critic trained with DD-PPO for 100M steps with dense shaped rewards. TP-SRL uses a STRIPS planner over RL skills (Pick, Place, Open/Close fridge, Open/Close drawer, Navigate), each skill trained on 5,000 configurations. SPA and TP-SPA use point-cloud mapping + IK goal sampling + BiRRT (RRTConnect, OMPL) + PD execution. SPA-Priv is the same with ground-truth geometry and a perfect controller.

setting.backbone: Small CNN visual encoder + state MLP + LSTM actor-critic trained from scratch with DD-PPO (MonolithicRL and TP-SRL skills). Non-learned SPA baselines use STRIPS + BiRRT/RRTConnect (OMPL).
setting.training_data: On-policy RL in Habitat 2.0 / ReplicaCAD scenes with YCB objects (9 train objects, 7 train receptacles for Pick). 100M steps per policy (70M for sensor ablations). Each skill uses 5,000 training configurations; the MonolithicRL full-task policy uses 5,000 task configurations. SPA needs no training.
setting.observation: Head- and arm-mounted RGB-D cameras (90° FoV, 128x128; skills use depth), arm joint proprioception, end-effector position, base egomotion (GPS+compass), and GeometricGoal 3D start/goal object positions
setting.action_space: Continuous end-effector delta (max 1.5 cm/step at 30 Hz, IK + PD) plus a scalar abstracted grasp/release. Base linear/angular velocity; the Navigate skill discretizes this into 20 velocity cells, with 0/0 as the stop action.
setting.simulator: Habitat 2.0 (Bullet physics + Magnum renderer) with ReplicaCAD scenes
setting.privileged: The goal is given as the ground-truth 3D center of mass of target objects (GeometricGoal); no maps or object models are given. TP-SRL/TP-SPA assume a perfect STRIPS task planner and known initial containment. Some variants use oracle navigation. SPA uses perfect localization to accumulate point clouds. SPA-Priv uses ground-truth scene geometry and a perfect (kinematic) controller.

numbers_note: The only results table for agents is the Pick generalization table (Table 3). All Home Assistant Benchmark (TidyHouse, PrepareGroceries, SetTable) results for MonolithicRL / TP-SRL / TP-SPA / TP-SPA-Priv, with learned and oracle navigation, are shown only as progressive-success plots (Fig. 7, 100 episodes on unseen layouts). The same holds for skill learning curves, camera-placement and time-delay analyses. Only a few figure values are quoted in text: head+arm camera 92%, arm-only 85%, sighted SCT >80%, and learned nav termination about -20%. Simulator throughput (SPS) is in Table 2 and is not an agent metric. No standard navigation benchmark is evaluated.
results: Habitat 2.0 simulates Fetch in ReplicaCAD at 1191 SPS single-process, 8186 SPS on 1 GPU and 25734 SPS on an 8-GPU node (idle). With all optimizations disabled it runs at 242 SPS single-process, versus iGibson's reported 100 SPS; other simulators report 10-400 SPS. On Pick, MonolithicRL reaches 91.7% on seen and 86.3% on unseen layouts, beating SPA (72.7%) and even privileged SPA-Priv (80.0%). It generalizes poorly to unseen receptacles (52.7% vs SPA 60.3%). On the long-horizon HAB tasks, flat RL performs abysmally and the task-planner + RL-skills hierarchy is much better. However, compounding errors, hand-off problems and learned navigation cause large drops. TP-SPA beats TP-SRL only on TidyHouse with oracle navigation and loses in the cluttered fridge task.
limitations: Full HAB tasks remain largely unsolved: hierarchical baselines rely on a perfect STRIPS task planner and known containment, oracle-navigation variants are needed for analysis, and results are reported mostly as progressive partial-success plots over 100 episodes.
Abstracted (snap) grasping, kinematic navmesh base motion, rigid-body only (no deformables, audio or tactile); ReplicaCAD is a single apartment (USA) with 111 layouts, limiting scene diversity.
End-to-end training throughput is still bottlenecked by environment synchronization and asset reloading on reset; no real-robot validation.
